source.title: Transformer-Based Approaches for Sensor-Based Human Activity Recognition: Opportunities and Challenges
source.authors: C. Leite; Henry Mauranen; Aziza Zhanabatyrova; Yu Xiao

record.file_problem: Supplied full text; opening abstract contains a line-break/word-joining artifact, but it does not prevent extraction.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares transformer and non-transformer HAR architectures and measures generalization-related performance and sharpness, using its own implementations and analysis rather than the claim versions’ original experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper tests image-independent HAR architecture performance, SAM, measured sharpness, quantization, and adversarial robustness. It does not test random-label memorization, widening past interpolation, optimizer comparisons, batch size, dropout, or memorized-example removal. Quantization and adversarial results are included only where they directly bear on measured sharpness and generalization-related robustness; their rows do not establish the claim’s train/test generalization gap.
record.test_reason: The study measures HAR test F1, loss landscapes, Hessian sharpness, adversarial robustness and quantization losses. None measures a claim version. In particular, V7 concerns magnitude-aware sharpness ranking train–test gaps within a convolutional family at similarly low training loss; this study compares different architectures using test F1 without reporting training losses or generalization gaps.
record.authors_conclusion: The record is broadly accurate: the authors find that their transformer HAR implementations generally underperform recurrent/convolutional counterparts, require greater computational effort, and can suffer substantial quantization losses and adversarial vulnerability. SAM helps most architectures on average but does not generally close the performance gap. Their sharpness–performance association is explicitly moderate and inconsistent. They argue that larger datasets and improved training, robustness and efficiency methods are needed; they do not establish V7's relationship with train–test gaps.
record.recipe_differences: Sensor-based activity recognition rather than the claim's random-label memorization, width sweeps, image architecture, optimizer, batch-size, dropout, or memorized-example experiments; six HAR datasets and a 20-epoch cap.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset affects SAM: performance improvement is greater on larger datasets, average degradation of 1.3% on Skoda, and less than 1% average improvement on OpportunityML. Architecture affects sharpness and quantization/adversarial robustness. SAM gains vary by architecture and dataset.

fits_no_version.finding: Under the tested HAR recipe, ResBiLSTM exceeds transformer variants in 82 of 84 comparisons; the two exceptions are ViT-SAM on Skoda and TASKED-SAM on PAMAP2.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The tested transformer HAR implementations usually achieve lower test weighted F1 than the recurrent/convolutional baseline within the 20-epoch training cap.

fits_no_version.finding: The authors report a moderate, inconsistent relationship between measured sharpness and test performance across architectures; TASKED is sharper yet performs better than several alternatives.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Hessian sharpness and normalized landscape shape have an imperfect association with test F1 across the tested HAR architectures.

fits_no_version.finding: SAM improves average performance for most transformer architectures, with RetNet an exception; benefits vary with dataset, including average degradation on Skoda.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAM's effect on HAR test F1 depends on architecture and dataset.

fits_no_version.finding: OpportunityML FGSM degradation is 1.89 percentage points for TEHAR and 3.51 for TTN, rather than the quantization values recorded as attack results.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sensitivity to adversarial input perturbations varies across HAR architectures.

fits_no_version.finding: OpportunityML INT8 degradation is 3.29 percentage points for ResBiLSTM and 85.59 for TTN.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Some transformer HAR architectures suffer substantially greater quantization losses than recurrent/convolutional baselines.

record.problems: Training was capped at 20 epochs; the paper does not report train-error/test-error gaps. Some aggregate sharpness and performance relationships are figure-based without exact numeric values. TASKED's adversarial training and subject discriminator were omitted from the implementation. No uncertainty estimates are reported for the extracted results.
record.rows_left_out: Table 2 reports results for six datasets and 16 architecture conditions; only OpportunityHL rows are transcribed here to illustrate the performance comparison, and the text's explicit aggregate statement is retained in R25. Table 3 and Table 4 contain additional model-by-dataset values; only OpportunityML examples are retained, along with the stated aggregate claims. The complete table grids would exceed the 60-row limit if expanded across all measurements, model conditions, and datasets.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting, natural-label held-out accuracy and chance-level random-label held-out accuracy under matched recipes.
Width sweeps beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the role of local connectivity or convolutional initialization.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning; SAM with Adam versus Adam does not establish this comparison.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that recover performance.
Dropout interventions and their dependence on dataset size, augmentation and weight decay.

Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance versus train–test gaps among similarly fitted networks of one convolutional family, including ranking against norm and margin measures. Filter-normalized landscape visualizations do not supply these comparisons.
Removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples and measuring the resulting test-accuracy loss.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's designation of V7 as tested is incorrect. These related sharpness findings warrant no support, scope-limit or challenge verdict on V7. Numerical figure values cannot be recovered from the supplied text, but the qualitative conclusions are stated explicitly.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label test performance under the same recipes.
Width sweeps beyond interpolation on MNIST or downsampled CIFAR-10.
Convolutional versus fully connected comparisons on image datasets; local connectivity and learned sparse connections.
Adaptive optimizer versus SGD comparisons on image or language benchmarks.
Large versus small batch training under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Dropout comparisons and interactions with data augmentation or weight decay.
Magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness, ranking against norm- and margin-based measures, and the stated CIFAR-10/SVHN settings.
Removing highly memorized training examples and measuring test accuracy, including the ResNet-50 datasets.
